# Bitcoin's Required Return: Market Risk, Concentration and Mortality

> Code, data and stored results of a working paper that asks what return Bitcoin's holders should
> require for the market, concentration and mortality risk they carry (the MCM equation), tests the
> answer against delivered returns month by month, and takes a census of cryptoasset deaths. The
> manuscript is in paper/.

Replication package by Agisilaos Papadogiannis (https://github.com/apapadogiannis).
Working paper: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7705239
Code and data: https://github.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-required-return  Archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24003938
Version 3.0.0, released 2026-11-25. A package is a fixed record: it changes only by a new
release, and a release that changes a reported number gets a new major version.
This file is written for AI agents and other programs. People should start at the README.

## Coverage

- The required return on Bitcoin at every month-end from January 2012 to the end of the data: lower
  edge, midpoint and upper edge of the band, with the inputs (outputs/required_band_monthly.csv).
- The monthly test: the required return against the return of the following month, by period
  (outputs/monthly_test.txt).
- The census: every cryptoasset in the Coin Metrics community dataset from 2010 to 24 May 2026,
  with birth, death, kind of death and size (outputs/panel_v3.csv; assets ever in the top twenty in
  outputs/elite_top20_curated.csv).
- The same equation for Ether and other cryptoassets, with equity indices and gold for comparison,
  and the table restated for a euro investor (outputs/cross_section_terms.txt,
  outputs/euro_table.txt).
- The robustness results of the appendices, one text file each in outputs/. The README lists which
  script writes which file and where it appears in the paper.

## Headline figures

As printed in the paper. Each is one of the checks in outputs/results.json.

- Required return on Bitcoin for its current holders, 2026: 18.1 percent a year (the median over
  the input ranges; a simple yearly rate, not a compound one) (90% range of the input uncertainty
  15.2 to 21.8). Section 4 and Appendix D.1.
- Monthly band for Bitcoin at the end of May 2026, midpoint: 19 percent a year (band 12 to 25).
  Section 5, Table 4.
- Required return on Ether for the average crypto owner: 23 percent a year (90% range 19 to 29).
  Section 6, Table 6.
- Delivered less required return at the midpoint, 2012 to 2026: 51 points a year, average of
  monthly returns (standard error 39). Section 5, Table 5.
- Delivered less required return at the midpoint, 2018 to 2026: 15 points a year, average of
  monthly returns (standard error 23). Section 5, Table 5.
- Cryptoassets in the census: 1624 assets. Section 3.
- Of which died: 471 assets. Section 3.
- Death rate of assets that were ever in the top twenty by trading volume, any cause: 3.46 percent
  a year. Section 3.
- Death rate of those assets by sudden collapse: 0.3 percent a year. Section 3.
- Bitcoin's volatility used for May 2026: 42 percent a year. Section 5, Table 4.
- Bitcoin's beta to the US equity market, May 2026: 1.75 (a ratio). Section 5, Table 4.
- Required return on Bitcoin for a holder with a negligible weight (the floor): 14 percent a year
  (90% range 12 to 16). Section 6, Table 6.
- Death rate of the smallest quarter of assets by size: 16.2 percent a year. Section 3.
- Death rate of the largest quarter of assets by size: 2.8 percent a year. Section 3.

## What this adds over reading the paper or recomputing

1. The death of an asset is not in any data feed. The census classifies each one by a stated rule
   (end of the feed, price collapse without recovery, volume collapse without recovery), treats
   ticker migrations as survivals, and enters the known sudden collapses at their public-record
   dates. The flags for every asset are in outputs/panel_v3.csv.
2. The share of wealth that holders keep in Bitcoin, which drives the concentration term, is taken
   from a household survey and held at that value, because repeated surveys of what owners hold
   show holdings per owner moving little with the price (data/holder_surveys.csv, with its
   sources). Documented fund and company holdings are added. The construction is in
   scripts/22_pretty_figs.py; scripts/49_holder_surveys.py and scripts/50_holder_weight_variants.py
   give the survey evidence and the other choices for the weight.
3. Dates are kept honest. A required return is dated at the month-end it is set and compared with
   the return of the following month.
4. The input data are stored in the repository with a checksum for every Coin Metrics file. The
   upstream archive stopped updating on 24 May 2026, so this copy is its last state and the run
   needs no download.
5. `census_checks`: 94 figures quoted in the paper, recomputed from the data and compared with the
   paper's figure; 94 agree exactly. The run fails if any does not.
6. `model_checks`: 1,228 figures quoted in the paper, recomputed from the data and compared with
   the paper's figure; 1,228 agree within the stated tolerance. The run fails if any does not.
7. The results are stored as they were when the paper's numbers were taken from them. A check
   reruns the code on the stored data and compares every stored result file with the fresh one,
   number by number (relative tolerance 1e-9; text and whole numbers exactly). It runs on every
   change and once a month, and the badge in the README shows the last run.

## Labels of the checks

The checks keep the audit script's short labels. What the recurring words and prefixes mean:

- lo, mid, hi: lower edge, midpoint and upper edge of the required-return band
- gap: delivered return less required return, in points a year
- se: standard error
- MC: the propagation of the input ranges by random draws (Section 4, Appendix D.1): median and
  percentiles of the required return
- T3, T4, T5: Tables 3, 4 and 5 of the paper
- Table 6, S6: Table 6 and Section 6: Ether and other cryptoassets
- S5, S7: Sections 5 and 7
- monthly: the monthly test of Section 5: the required return at a month-end against the return of
  the following month
- grouping: the monthly test with the months grouped in other ways (Appendix D)
- compound: the table of compound returns: the arithmetic required return less the drag of
  volatility
- RV, Sharpe, sizing, rebalanced: what the required return means for an investor: return per unit
  of risk, a small rebalanced position, and returns net of the death rate
- w: the share of wealth a holder keeps in the asset, the weight of the concentration term
- kappa: correlation of an asset with the crypto market times market volatility over asset
  volatility; it scales the crypto share into the asset's weight
- gamma: risk aversion
- conc: the concentration term
- rf, TNX: the risk-free rate; TNX is the ten-year Treasury yield
- elite: an asset that was ever in the top twenty by trading volume
- jump: a sudden collapse, as against a slow death by abandonment or delisting
- core universe: the census after stablecoins, tokenised stocks and wrapped assets are set aside
- curated: deaths after ticker migrations are removed and the known collapses are entered at their
  public dates
- exposure: asset-years at risk
- size Q1 to Q4: quarters of assets by size, Q1 the smallest
- n: a count of assets, months or windows
- letter and number prefixes (A.3, D.4, E.4 and so on): an appendix section of the paper. A few
  follow the numbering of an earlier draft (E.2, Fig6) and do not match a section of the current
  paper; for those, the README's table of scripts says where the result appears
- age rule: the rule of thumb that the expected return falls as one over Bitcoin's age, which the
  paper compares with the required return

## Files

- outputs/results.json: a `headline` list with the figures most often asked for, then every number
  the paper quotes that the code recomputes, as two lists of checks. `census_checks`: claim,
  computed value, the paper's figure. `model_checks`: the same with the tolerance, which reflects
  the rounding of the printed figure. The labels are the audit script's own short names (T4 is
  Table 4, S6 Section 6, A.7 Appendix A.7, MC the propagation of the input ranges, elite an asset
  ever in the top twenty, jump a sudden collapse); the README says which script and table each
  group belongs to. It holds 1,322 checks, and under `package` the paper, the identifiers, the
  version, the licence and the citation. Start with its `headline` list, which is repeated below.
- outputs/required_band_monthly.csv: one row per month-end: age, risk-free rate, volatility, beta,
  holder weight at both edges, the band and the age rule.
- outputs/panel_v3.csv: one row per asset: birth, last observation, the death flags and dates under
  each definition.
- outputs/*.txt: the result tables as printed for the paper. Use results.json to quote a number and
  these to see its table.
- paper/manuscript.pdf: the working paper.
- outputs/holder_weight_variants.txt: the band and the monthly test with the owners' weight held at
  19% (the paper's choice), at 12% and at 8%, and with a weight that follows the market value.
- data/: all inputs. data/cmdata/MANIFEST.sha256 lists the checksums; data/holder_surveys.csv holds
  the survey figures on what owners hold, with its sources in data/holder_surveys_SOURCE.md.

Raw files: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-required-return/main/<path>, for example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-required-return/main/outputs/results.json

## How to read the figures

- A required return is what holders should require for the risk they carry. It is not a forecast of
  what Bitcoin will return.
- For the monthly path, quote the midpoint together with its band. The band is wide in the early
  years because the holder's weight was high and volatility extreme.
- In results.json `paper` is the figure as printed, usually rounded; `computed` is the value the
  code gives, at full precision where it is calculated and with the table's rounding where it is
  read from a printed table. Quote `paper` when citing the paper.
- A check whose claim is a statement and not a quantity has `paper` 1 and `computed` 1: read it as
  true.
- Not every `paper` value is a printed figure. Where a check tests an identity or a formula,
  `paper` holds the other side of the identity at full precision; where the paper says "about",
  `paper` holds the round figure and the tolerance is wide. A wide tolerance means the paper's
  statement is approximate, so quote `computed` for the exact value.
- The same quantity can appear in more than one check, at different rounding or from different
  tables (a beta of 1.5 in the text and 1.51 in a table; for Ether a median of 23.0 and a sum of
  terms of 23.4). Prefer the headline list; otherwise say which table the figure is from.
- Outside the headline list, the printed tables in outputs/*.txt, with their row and column
  headings, are often the clearer source; the checks tell you the figure was recomputed.
- The paper's 2026 figure for Bitcoin is the median when the uncertain inputs are drawn across
  their ranges. The monthly band's midpoint (the T4 checks, required_band_monthly.csv, and the
  Crypto Observatory) averages the two edges of the band at that month's risk-free rate and can
  differ from it by a point or so at the same date. They are different figures; say which one you
  quote.
- The many checks labelled as sensitivities (other weights, other premia, other windows) are
  robustness results, not the paper's headline.
- In required_band_monthly.csv rates are fractions a year, not percent.
- Realized averages over short periods have large standard errors, which outputs/monthly_test.txt
  reports beside each one.

## Do not use this for

- A forecast, a price target or a view on whether to hold Bitcoin.
- Anything after the paper's dates. The cryptoasset data end on 24 May 2026 and the package is not
  updated.
- Commercial reuse of the Coin Metrics data.
- The fate of a single asset. The census gives rates for groups of assets.
- Current figures. Use the live tool: Crypto Observatory,
  https://apapadogiannis.github.io/crypto-observatory/ (the same equation recomputed each month
  from live sources, with the differences from this paper's sources stated; guide at
  https://apapadogiannis.github.io/crypto-observatory/llms.txt)

## Source, licence and credit

The results in outputs/ are released under CC BY 4.0
(https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The licence allows any reuse and has one condition:
credit. If you use a figure from this package in an answer, a report or a data set, cite the paper.
The code is under the MIT License.

The cryptoasset data in data/cmdata are an unmodified copy of the Coin Metrics community dataset,
licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial use, with attribution). They keep that licence and are not
covered by the licence above. ETF prices, the euro/dollar rate and the Treasury yield are from
Yahoo Finance and are included for replication only.

Cite as: Papadogiannis, A. (2026). Bitcoin's Required Return: Market Risk, Concentration and Mortality. Working paper. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7705239

The package itself: Papadogiannis, A. (2026). Bitcoin's Required Return: Market Risk, Concentration and Mortality. Replication package, version 3.0.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24003938

To describe the source in a sentence: Papadogiannis (2026), "Bitcoin's Required Return: Market
Risk, Concentration and Mortality", working paper, with its replication package.

The same licence and citation are inside outputs/results.json, under `package`.
